prize_parts.citation: for introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, and thereby transforming the analysis of exporting, foreign investment, reallocation and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged after the exchange. B012 is a discovery with a specific mechanism. Trade opening forces selection across heterogeneous firms and reallocates activity toward the more productive ones. That adds a channel for the gains from trade that representative-firm models could not generate. It is also the kind of contribution I weight most: a model built to explain firm-level facts, then tested on new microdata for two decades. Those tests cover exporter premia, selection into exporting, and the export-versus-FDI choice in Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple. The framework is now the standard base for trade, productivity and reallocation analysis, and it fed quantitative and macro work. Attribution at two names is as tight as any ballot with a trade theme. Melitz (2003) is the originating model, and Helpman made it a general programme and extended it to the organisation of firms. The citation now says 'exporting, foreign investment, reallocation' so that the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple strand is named explicitly. I do not rest the case on trade's absence from the prize since 2008, which is a timing consideration and not merit. I also do not rest it on first-place counts. B012 has three explicit supporters, B022 has five, and neither number is evidence about the science.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is credit beyond the named pair. Bernard and Jensen established the exporter facts, and Eaton and Kortum built a parallel heterogeneous-producer framework. A two-name award would be read as understating them, and the three-name cap cannot fix that. Welfare conclusions from quantitative versions depend on functional form, notably the Pareto productivity assumption, so the 'gains from trade' part of the citation is partly model-dependent. Helpman also appears on B007, so the Committee would be choosing which body of his work to honour. My own assessment is not decisive against B022 on common criteria. B022 has the more transparent identification and a first-order policy question about who bears adjustment costs. The case against B012 is that it is a theory-and-structure prize whose core insight is already settled, while B022 is a prize about people and places that the Committee could judge more consequential. That is a legitimate difference in weighting, not an error by either side.

responses.point: Hassler moved to B012 from B021 on attribution grounds. He backs the Melitz-Helpman pair and notes that Redding's quantitative and spatial work, Bernard-Jensen, and Eaton-Kortum all have claims. He also notes that welfare results are sensitive to parametric assumptions.
responses.response: I agree with the pair and with his reason for leaving B021, since attribution on the three-name cut is the right test. On Redding, I would still keep him off. His quantitative and spatial extensions build on a selection mechanism that later work has not revised. A third name would also widen the citation toward quantitative welfare claims, which is where the functional-form sensitivity he flags is greatest. I would put the selection and reallocation mechanism in the citation and leave the welfare magnitudes to the Scientific Background. I also agree that Helpman can be named only once, so B012 and B007 should not be combined.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B022 first and says B012 and B022 are not competitors, because trade theory and the distributional consequences of shocks cover different ground. He would not stand in the way of B012 if the Committee wants to recognise trade, but judges B022 to have greater explanatory reach for people and places.
responses.response: I agree they cover different ground, so a head-to-head comparison is only possible on the common criteria: originality, breadth of confirmation, and attributable credit. On those I still give B012 a modest edge. Its core insight has not been revised by later work. The B022 debate is about the size and persistence of effects, and that debate is open even though the existence of adjustment costs is not. Teorell's explanatory-reach argument is a legitimate weighting, though, and I do not consider it a lesser criterion. I have moved B022 to the first position among my alternatives. The reason is the clean Autor-Dorn-Hanson attribution and the decade of replication and critique, not the support count.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B022 first with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. She argues that the China-shock evidence is the best-documented and most replicated strand, that Dorn is a full co-author, and that magnitudes and persistence remain contested. She also flags overlap with the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes.
responses.response: I accept that Dorn belongs with Autor and Hanson on a citation built on the trade-shock evidence. If B022 is chosen, my version is the trio, and I would not narrow it to two. I share her caution on the contested persistence estimates. I would want the Scientific Background to address the shift-share critiques and re-analyses directly, and I would word the citation around the empirical evidence on how technology and import competition reshape labour demand and local labour markets, not around the task-model theory whose originators are outside the credited set. I read the thematic proximity to recent prizes as a mild timing consideration. It is not a merit objection, and B012 faces no comparable proximity.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B043 first with Kiyotaki and Moore only. He says B012 would be at least as defensible if breadth of confirmed use is weighted more heavily, that his case rests largely on one theoretical paper, and that direct identification of collateral-driven amplification is debated.
responses.response: I agree that the two-name Kiyotaki-Moore version is the right size, and I no longer propose adding Gertler. He is also right that the mechanism is distinct from the bank-run and crisis work recognised in 2022. His own list of weaknesses is why I keep B012 ahead. The core mechanism rests on one originating paper, and its empirical identification is still debated. B012's confirmation on firm-level microdata is broader. I keep B043 as my second alternative. I would support it over B012 only if the Committee concluded that the amplification mechanism is better identified than the evidence I know supports, and I cannot establish that from the supplied files.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee should weigh the Bernard-Jensen and Eaton-Kortum contributions more heavily than a two-name citation allows, and whether a citation can name the selection mechanism without overstating the pair's priority.
Whether the functional-form sensitivity of quantitative welfare results should reduce the weight on the gains-from-trade part of the citation.

Whether the Committee prefers to recognise the distributional and labour-market consequences of trade and technology (B022) over the trade-theory foundation (B012). That is a weighting of criteria I cannot settle from the files.
Whether Helpman is better honoured through B012 or B007, since only one prize can name him.
My attribution judgements rest on general knowledge of the literature and the colleagues' round-1 statements. I have not independently verified them.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent for the preferred B012 (Helpman and Melitz) or for the alternatives B022 (Autor, Hanson, Dorn) and B043 (Kiyotaki, Moore) from the supplied profile. My research is in corporate finance, and my listed co-authors (Kaplan, Axelson, Weisbach, Jenkinson, Lerner and others) are not credited names on those ballots. I disclose my adjunct professorship at Chicago Booth, my KVA vice-presidency, and my long overlap on the Committee with Hassler, Krusell, Ellingsen and Svensson. None is a specific tie to a candidate. These are disclosed, not adjudicated.
